Fwiw -- if you just look at AI related business investment, it contributed 1.53 to Q1 GDP

Intellectual Property products: 0.70
Information Processing equipment: 0.83

Business investment contributed **more** to GDP in Q1 than consumer spending.

This is an AI economy now.

Business investment contribution to Q1 GDP: 1.48
Personal consumption contribution to Q1 GDP: 1.08

(Joey's great chart shows the biz investment in green vs. consumption in yellow)


Joey Politano 🏳️‍🌈 (@JosephPolitano)

NEW: 

US Real GDP came in at a 2% annualized growth rate in Q1 2026 data released this morning. Consumption & investment increased, government output rose, and the tra

Important: The US savings rate fell to 3.6% in March. That's the lowest since fall 2022 (the "revenge spend" era). And it's frankly one of the lower readings of all time.

American households are getting squeezed.
Many are not able to save right now as they face ongoing high costs for gas, electricity, and healthcare.

Bottom line: There's less cushion if a downturn or economic slowdown occurs.

This is the AI economy now.
Just incredible to see the +10.4% jump in business investment in Q1. That's the highest since Q2 2023 (when the big semiconductor factory buildout was underway. Now it's all AI)

Notice consumption: +1.6%. That's pretty tepid. One of the weaker consumer spending readings lately.

JUST IN: PCE Inflation jumped to 3.5% in March, the highest in three years (since May 2023). This is a direct result of the war in Iran. And the pain will almost certainly be worse in April and (likely) May.

Core PCE Inflation (excluding food and energy) jumped to 3.2% --> highest since January 2024.

This is mainly a gas story, but healthcare also showing some spending increase.

JUST IN: The US economy grew at a 2% pace in Q1, driven by a massive surge in business investment.

Nonresidential business jumped +10.4% in Q1 due to a boom in AI spending and equipment investment.

Consumption grew a tepid +1.6% (it's the slowest consumer spending in a year).

**We need to watch the US consumer. Consumption was already slowing before the war in Iran and is likely to slow more as people deal with high gas prices**

Oof. The US national gas average just hit $4.30, according to AAA. That's the highest since July 2022.

Gas prices have shot up $1.40 since the war in Iran began. That's adding ~$70 extra a month to household costs. 

#gas #inflation
Fed Chair Powell says the Supreme Court's Lisa Cook decision is NOT a factor in his decision to stay/go.

Fed Chair Powell on his decisions to stay as a Fed Governor: "Things that happened in last 3 months left me no choice but to see them through at least that long."


Heather Long (@byHeatherLong)

BIG NEWS: Fed Chair Powell will stay on as a governor after his chair term ends on May 15.

"I will continue to serve as a governor for a period for time to be determined. I plan to keep a low profile as a governor," Chair Powell says.

He says there are "ongoing legal threats" to Fed independence.

BIG NEWS: Fed Chair Powell will stay on as a governor after his chair term ends on May 15.

"I will continue to serve as a governor for a period for time to be determined. I plan to keep a low profile as a governor," Chair Powell says.

He says there are "ongoing legal threats" to Fed independence.

JUST IN: The Federal Reserve didn’t change interest rates. The target range is still 3.5 to 3.75%, where it’s been since December.

But big news: The decision was 8 to 4.
We haven't seen that much dissent since 1992

Yes, 11 of the 12 supported leaving rates unchanged, but Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie Logan “did not support inclusion of an easing bias in the statement at this time.” [In other words, they think the Fed's next move might be a rate HIKE]

Fed/Trump official Stephen Miran

Rystad Energy says it will take until July for roughly normal flows through the Strait of Hormuz

"Our analysis shows that it would take until July for oil flows to normalize to some 80-90% of pre-war production levels, and another 1-2 months for those barrels start showing up at ports for processing into the most urgently needed products."

NEW from me: The White House (and many economists) expected $700 to $1,000 higher refunds, on average. 

The reality is closer to $375.

Bottom line: Yes, refunds are higher in 2026 (and likely to be the highest ever). But it's less of a spending boost (and cushion against higher gas prices) than many expected. 

economyheather.substack.com/…

Something feels off here...
S&P 500 has gained back *all* of its losses due to war in Iran. After the rally today, the index is within a hair of its record closing high of 6,978.60 on January 27.

Wall Street investors are looking beyond the war already, even though there's no final deal yet. (And we still don't know who will control the Strait of Hormuz when the war does end).

There's still a lot of tail risk.
